analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Arctic Refuge oil leasing program and designates the coastal plain as wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee since it was referred there on April 29, 2025, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the section of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act that created an oil and gas leasing program in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, and it would designate roughly 1.56 million acres of that coastal plain as federal wilderness, which permanently bans roads, vehicles, and development there. That would take oil and gas drilling in the refuge off the table. The bill has not moved since being referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who value protected public lands, including Alaska Native communities like the Gwich'in who depend on the coastal plain's caribou herds, gain permanent protection from drilling and the roads, seismic testing, and spills that come with it. Future generations keep the refuge undeveloped, and the federal government avoids leasing a public resource at potentially bargain prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public-lands users and Alaska Native communities

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 20001 of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the provision that created a mandatory oil and gas program for the Arctic Refuge, eliminating the legal mandate to sell leases there.

Designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, which bars permanent roads, motorized vehicles, and commercial development in the area permanently.

Places the land under the same wilderness management rules as the rest of the Arctic Refuge already designated, so the coastal plain cannot be opened to drilling by a future administration without another act of Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to what they see as a promising drilling frontier on the coastal plain, and the State of Alaska and the federal treasury lose the revenue-sharing from lease sales that the 2017 tax law promised. Anyone who would have benefited from lower-energy-price arguments for the refuge's oil also loses the option, though refuge oil would be a small share of national supply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies, Alaska, and federal lease revenue

drawbacks.text: The repeal cancels projected federal and Alaska revenue: the 2017 tax law directed lease-sale proceeds partly to the federal government and partly to the State of Alaska, so repeal forgoes that money at a time when Alaska relies heavily on resource revenue.

Supporters of the 2017 program argue that domestic drilling improves energy security and lowers prices, and wilderness designation forecloses that option permanently rather than leaving it to future administrations to weigh.

A bill from the minority party with one Republican cosponsor cannot become law in this Congress, so the effort spends political capital without changing the legal status of the refuge in the near term.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who prioritize protecting a largely untouched Arctic ecosystem, the bill's permanent protection outweighs the forgone lease revenue, which was speculative and modest relative to the federal budget. For Alaska, which shares in lease proceeds, and for the oil industry, the loss is concrete. The bill does not attempt a compromise; it simply reverses the 2017 mandate and locks in protection, which is exactly why it has no support beyond one Republican.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on April 29, 2025, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the Arctic Refuge Protection Act in the House on April 29, 2025, with 108 Democratic cosponsors and one Republican cosponsor listed.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, where a bill must receive a hearing and a vote from the committee before the full House can consider it.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action has been scheduled or taken in the roughly eight months since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the status quo holds: the 2017 drilling program remains on the books but the refuge has not been developed, so the oil industry retains the legal path to leases while conservationists retain the legislative option to block them.

for.name: Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Arctic Refuge oil and gas program and designate the coastal plain as wilderness.

for.name: 108 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it roughly half the House Democratic caucus in support.

sides.party_line_note: All 109 cosponsors are Democrats except one Republican, and Republicans hold a 223-seat House majority and control the Natural Resources Committee, where the bill has sat without action since April 2025 [S3][S1].

industries.note: The bill repeals the legal program that would sell them leases to drill in the Arctic Refuge coastal plain and permanently bars development there. Their interest in drilling a protected public refuge runs against the conservation interest the bill serves for the public.

The 2017 law directed a share of Arctic Refuge lease proceeds to Alaska; repeal cancels that revenue stream. Residents of the state are split between resource revenue and the refuge's value for subsistence hunting and tourism.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans controlling the House and the Natural Resources Committee, and the drilling program having been created by a Republican-authored 2017 tax law, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or vote in this Congress. It will probably sit in committee and expire unless the chamber's agenda shifts.
